title: Telling it well
cando: tell a detailed account, and report fairly what others said and meant

about.text: In this lesson you tell a story over dinner and make your friends want to hear the end. You use the four perfect forms to make the order of events clear, and verbs like claimed, admitted, urged and denied to report what people said. Then you read a witness statement and meeting minutes, and write one event from two points of view.
goals: Tell a story that keeps people listening, with You'll never believe…, It turned out that… and Apparently…
Use the four perfect forms to show what happened first, and for how long.
Report what people said fairly, with verbs like claimed, admitted, urged and denied.
Read a witness statement and meeting minutes, and write one event from two points of view.
Retell a story you heard, reporting fairly what each person said and meant.

chapters.title: A story over dinner
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you tell a story. Not a report, but the kind of story you tell friends over dinner.
Listen to Mei. She tells her friend Omar about a strange morning at work. Notice how she starts: You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday. That makes Omar want to hear the rest.
Then listen for two useful phrases. It turned out that… gives the surprise, the thing that was really true. It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station.
Apparently… tells people you heard this from someone else, so you can't be completely sure. Apparently, my manager had put the wrong station in the email.
Good storytellers also leave out the boring parts. To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late.

chapters.title: Four perfect forms, and fair reporting
chapters.text:
The grammar in this lesson has two parts.
The first is the four perfect forms. Two of them reach up to now. I've waited an hour: that's the fact. I've been waiting an hour: that's the activity, and how long it has gone on.
The other two reach up to a moment in the past. The meeting had started when I arrived. I'd been waiting for forty minutes when he rang.
So ask yourself two questions. Does it reach up to now, or up to a moment in the past? And do you mean the finished fact, or the activity going on?
The second part is reporting verbs. Said is neutral. Claimed suggests you're not sure it's true. Admitted means someone accepted something they didn't want to say. Urged means advised strongly. Denied means said it wasn't true.
Choose carefully. The verb you choose shows what you think.

chapters.title: Two sides of the story
chapters.text:
In Section 3, you read two documents about the same event at a warehouse: a witness statement, and the minutes of a meeting.
Read them side by side. Where do they agree? Where do they contradict each other? And is every verb fair, or does one of them take sides?
Look closely at the reporting verbs. Stated is neutral. Claimed is not, so ask yourself whether the writer had a reason to doubt.
Then you write about one event from two points of view. Tell it first as one person saw it, then as the other person saw it. Keep the order of events clear, and choose your reporting verbs carefully.

chapters.title: Retell a story you heard
chapters.text:
Then it's your turn. Think of a story someone told you: a friend, a colleague or a neighbour. Choose one with two or more people who didn't agree.
Retell it in the live class. Report what each person said, and also what they meant. Be fair to both sides.
If you're not sure something is true, say so: apparently, or she claimed.
Your listeners will ask you questions, so make sure you know the order of events.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story linked to this lesson.
As you read, ask yourself who is telling it. Is the storyteller fair to everyone? Would another person in the story tell it differently?

warmup.prompt: A friend starts a story with “You'll never believe what happened…”. How do you feel?
choices: curious: I want to hear it
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. A good opening makes people want to hear more. Mind you, some storytellers do exaggerate a little!

conversation.title: You'll never believe it
conversation.setting: Mei is having dinner with her friend Omar. She tells him about a mix-up at work last Friday, when she had to meet a new client at the station.
lines: You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday.
My manager asked me to meet a new client at the station. A Mr Adeyemi, coming from Birmingham for a big meeting.
That's what I thought. I'd been waiting on the platform for forty minutes, and there was no sign of him.
No! It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station, on the far side of town. Apparently, my manager had put the wrong station in the email.
What a mix-up! So how did you find him?
Well, believe it or not, I went into a café to ring him, and he was sitting at the next table. He'd taken a taxi to come and find me!
To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late for the meeting. At first my manager denied it was her fault. She claimed the email was perfectly clear.
Not at all. She's since admitted her mistake. Luckily, Mr Adeyemi thought it was hilarious. He's been telling everyone the story ever since.

questions.q: Why couldn't Mei find Mr Adeyemi at first?
questions.a: He was waiting at a different station.
wrong: He had gone straight to the office.
questions.why: Mei says: It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station.
The manager put the wrong station in the email, and she has since admitted it.

questions.q: How did Mr Adeyemi feel about the mix-up?
wrong: He wanted to cancel the meeting.
questions.why: Mei says he thought it was hilarious.

phrases.text: You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday.
phrases.use: Starting a story so that people want to hear it.

phrases.text: It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station.
phrases.use: Giving the surprise: what was really true.

phrases.text: Apparently, my manager had put the wrong station in the email.
phrases.use: Passing on something you heard from someone else.

phrases.text: Believe it or not, he was sitting at the next table.
phrases.use: Introducing a surprising fact that is true.

phrases.text: To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late.
phrases.use: Skipping the less interesting details and getting to the end.
Reacting to a story about a confusion.
Showing that you want to hear the rest.

items.meaning: To be discovered to be true in the end, often as a surprise.
items.example: The stranger at the door turned out to be my new neighbour.

items.meaning: According to what you have heard or read, although you are not completely sure it is true.
items.example: Apparently, the office is closing for two weeks in August.

items.meaning: Used before you say something surprising that is true.
items.example: Believe it or not, I've never been on a plane.

items.meaning: Suddenly and unexpectedly, without any warning.
items.example: An old colleague rang me out of the blue and offered me a job.

items.w: to cut a long story short
items.meaning: Used when you skip the details and go straight to the ending.
items.example: To cut a long story short, we missed the flight and stayed another night.

items.meaning: To start a journey.
items.example: We set off at six to avoid the traffic.

items.meaning: To catch other people's conversation by chance, when they are not talking to you.
items.example: I overheard two managers talking about the new office in the lift.

items.meaning: Talk about other people's private lives, which is often unkind or not true.
items.example: Don't believe office gossip. Ask the person directly.

items.meaning: To make something sound bigger, better or worse than it really is.
items.example: He always exaggerates. Hundreds of people means about thirty.

items.meaning: When two things happen at the same time by chance, in a surprising way.
items.example: What a coincidence! My sister works there too.

items.meaning: A mistake that happens because someone confuses two things, times or people.
items.example: There was a mix-up with the dates, so two teams booked the same room.

items.meaning: Extremely funny.
items.example: His description of the meeting was hilarious.

items.meaning: Very strange and unusual, and difficult to explain.
items.example: It was a bizarre email: no subject, no name, just one word.

items.meaning: Extremely surprised.
items.example: I was astonished when she said she was leaving after twenty years.

items.meaning: To start making loud sounds suddenly, because something is very funny.
items.example: When the manager walked in wearing a paper crown, we all burst out laughing.

sound.title: Small, quick words: I'd been and I've been
sound.explain: In the perfect forms, the small words are short and quick, and the main verb is strong. I had becomes I'd, and been sounds like bin. I've been and I'd been sound very similar, so listen for the v or the d: it tells you whether the story reaches now or a moment in the past. Listen, then say each group and each line.
groups: I've been waiting · I'd been waiting
she's been working · she'd been working
lines: I'd been waiting on the platform for forty minutes.
It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station.
He's been telling everyone the story ever since.

sayIt.instructions: Say Mei's lines as if you were telling the story to a friend. Record yourself, then listen back. Is your voice lively? Are the small words short and quick?
lines: You'll never believe what happened to me on Friday.
That's what I thought. I'd been waiting on the platform for forty minutes, and there was no sign of him.
No! It turned out that he'd been waiting at the other station, on the far side of town.
To cut a long story short, we were twenty minutes late for the meeting.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from Mei's story. The first four use a perfect form. The last two report what someone said.
examples: I'd been waiting on the platform for forty minutes.
My manager had put the wrong station in the email.
He's been telling everyone the story ever since.
She claimed the email was perfectly clear.
At first my manager denied it was her fault.
spot.question: Which two perfect forms reach up to a moment in the past, and which two reach up to now? Which two describe an activity that went on for some time? And what does claimed tell you about Mei's opinion?
spot.answer: I'd been waiting and had put reach up to a moment in the past. She's admitted and he's been telling reach up to now. I'd been waiting and he's been telling describe an activity going on. Claimed shows that Mei doesn't believe it: the email was not clear. Denied means the manager said it wasn't her fault.

rules.title: The four perfect forms
rule: Up to now, the fact: I've waited an hour. He's told the story five times.
Up to now, the activity: I've been waiting an hour. He's been telling everyone.
Up to a moment in the past, the fact: When I arrived, the meeting had started.
Up to a moment in the past, the activity: I'd been waiting for forty minutes when he rang.
A number of finished things takes the simple form: I've sent three emails, not I've been sending three emails.
rules.mistake: Not: I had waiting for an hour. Say: I had been waiting for an hour. Don't lose the been.

rules.title: Reporting verbs that show a view: claimed, admitted, urged, denied
rule: Said, told and explained are neutral: they give no opinion.
Claimed suggests doubt: He claimed the email was clear. Maybe it wasn't.
Admitted means someone accepted something they would rather not say: She admitted her mistake.
Denied means said it wasn't true: He denied taking it. He denied that he took it.
Urged means advised strongly: She urged us to check the address.
rules.mistake: Not: He denied to take the money. Say: He denied taking the money. Admit works the same way: she admitted making a mistake.

practice.q: I ___ for forty minutes when he finally rang.
practice.why: An activity running up to a moment in the past: had been + -ing.

practice.q: She's exhausted. She ___ on that report all day.
practice.why: An activity up to now, with a result you can see: has been + -ing.

practice.q: By the time we arrived, the meeting ___ .
practice.why: Earlier than another past event: had + past participle.

practice.q: I ___ three emails to the supplier this week, and they still haven't replied.
practice.why: A number of finished things up to now takes the simple form: have sent.

practice.q: He's been telling that story ___ Friday.
practice.why: Since + the starting point: since Friday.

practice.q: They were tired because they ___ driving since six o'clock.
practice.why: An activity up to a moment in the past: had been + -ing.

practice.q: He ___ taking the money. He said it wasn't true.
practice.why: Deny means to say that something is not true.

practice.q: She ___ that she had made a mistake, and said sorry to everyone.
practice.why: Admit means to accept something you would rather not say.

practice.q: The doctor ___ me to rest for a week.
He ___ that the train was late, but we checked and it was on time.
practice.why: Claimed shows doubt: what he said may not be true.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a small mix-up or a surprise from your own life or work. Tell it in four or five sentences. Use at least two perfect forms, one of them with been, and one reporting verb: claimed, admitted, urged or denied.
yourTurn.model: You'll never believe what happened at my gym last week. I'd been waiting at reception for twenty minutes when a trainer finally came out. It turned out that my class had been moved to the afternoon. The receptionist claimed she had sent everyone a text. But when I showed her my phone, she admitted it had never arrived.

text.title: One delivery, two documents
text.body:
PRACTICE DOCUMENTS: these people and companies do not exist

WITNESS STATEMENT
Name: Amina Yusuf        Job: Warehouse assistant, Hollins Foods
Date of incident: Tuesday 4 March        Statement written: Wednesday 5 March

1. At about 7.40 a.m. I was checking stock near the loading bay. A van from Fastway Parcels had arrived at about 7.30, and the driver had been unloading for about ten minutes.
2. I heard a loud crash and turned round. A pallet of glass jars had fallen from the van's tail lift. I did not see what made it fall.
3. The driver told our supervisor, Tomasz Nowak, that the tail lift had been faulty for weeks. Tomasz said that the driver had loaded the pallet badly.
4. I recall that Tomasz asked the driver not to leave until the damage had been photographed. The driver agreed.
5. Nobody was hurt. I have written this statement from my own memory, and I have not discussed it with anyone.
Signed: A. Yusuf

---

MINUTES: DELIVERY REVIEW
Hollins Foods and Fastway Parcels, Friday 7 March
Present: Lena Fischer (Hollins, chair), Tomasz Nowak (Hollins), Kwame Mensah (Fastway driver), Priya Shah (Fastway manager)

1. Lena explained that 48 jars had been broken, with a value of £310.
2. Kwame stated that he had arrived at 7.15, and had been unloading for about twenty-five minutes when the tail lift dropped suddenly.
3. Kwame claimed that he had reported the fault with the tail lift twice in February. Priya confirmed that both reports had been received.
4. Tomasz stated that the pallet had been loaded badly. Kwame disputed this, and said that he had loaded it in the usual way.
5. Tomasz admitted that he had not seen the pallet fall.
6. Priya urged both companies to wait for an engineer's report on the tail lift before deciding who should pay.
Action: Priya to send the engineer's report to Lena by 14 March.

gist.q: What are the two documents about?
gist.a: a pallet of jars that fell during a delivery
wrong: a driver who arrived late for a meeting
a new tail lift for the warehouse
gist.why: Both describe the pallet of glass jars that fell from the van's tail lift.

gist.q: What has not been decided yet?
gist.a: who should pay for the damage
gist.why: Priya urged both companies to wait for the report before deciding who should pay.

detail.a: the fallen pallet, after she heard the crash
wrong: the driver loading the pallet badly
detail.why: She heard a crash, turned round and saw that the pallet had fallen. She did not see what made it fall.

detail.q: On which detail do the two documents not agree?
detail.why: Amina says the van arrived at about 7.30. In the minutes, Kwame says he arrived at 7.15.

detail.q: In item 3 of the minutes, why is the verb claimed unfair to Kwame?
detail.a: Priya confirmed that his reports had been received.
wrong: Kwame was not at the meeting.
The jars were not really broken.
detail.why: Claimed suggests doubt, but the reports were confirmed. A neutral verb, like stated, would be fairer.

detail.q: What did Priya urge both companies to do?
detail.a: wait for the engineer's report before deciding who pays
wrong: pay half of the cost each straight away
ask Amina to write a second statement
detail.why: Priya urged both companies to wait for an engineer's report on the tail lift.

items.meaning: A particular way of seeing a situation, shaped by your position or your experience.
items.example: From the driver's perspective, the tail lift was the problem.

items.meaning: One person's description of an event, which may be different from other people's.
items.example: The two drivers gave very different versions of the accident.

items.meaning: Seen, heard or experienced by you yourself, not heard from someone else.
items.example: Amina's account is first-hand: she was there.

items.meaning: The order in which a number of things happen.
items.example: Please describe the sequence of events, starting with the van's arrival.

items.meaning: To remember something, especially when you describe it to someone.
items.example: I don't recall the exact time, but it was before eight.

items.meaning: To say that something is not true or not correct.
items.example: The driver disputes the supervisor's version of events.

items.meaning: To say or show the opposite of what someone or something else says.
items.example: The photos contradict his claim that the boxes were already damaged.

items.meaning: The same each time, or agreeing with the other facts.
items.example: Her two statements are consistent: the times and the details match.

items.meaning: Unfairly supporting one side, because of your own feelings or interests.
items.example: The report was biased: it only included the manager's side.

items.meaning: Based on facts, not on your personal feelings or opinions.
items.example: Try to be objective. Write what you saw, not what you think.

items.meaning: Not supporting either side in an argument.
items.example: Stated is a neutral word, but claimed is not.

model.title: One event, two points of view
model.body:
Tomasz's version
On Tuesday morning, a Fastway driver was unloading glass jars at our loading bay. I had been watching the clock, because three more vans were due. Suddenly I heard a crash: a whole pallet had come off the tail lift. In my view, it had been loaded badly, because the jars were stacked too high. The driver said the tail lift had been faulty for weeks, but I had no way of checking that.

Kwame's version
On Tuesday morning, I had been unloading at Hollins Foods for about twenty-five minutes when the tail lift dropped suddenly. A pallet of jars fell and broke. I had reported that fault twice in February, and my manager has confirmed it. The supervisor told me I had loaded the pallet badly, but he has since admitted that he didn't see it fall.

write.task: Write about one event from two points of view. Choose an event from your own life or work: an argument, a mix-up or a small accident. It can be real or made up. Write one paragraph for each person, 60 to 80 words each. Use at least two perfect forms and two reporting verbs.
write.starter: …'s version: On … morning, I had been …
checklist: Each paragraph tells the event from one person's perspective.
The sequence of events is clear, with had or had been for the earlier events.
I used claimed or denied only where there is a real reason for doubt.
A reader can see where the two versions agree and where they contradict each other.

card.title: Retell a story you heard
card.situation: Someone told you a story recently: a friend, a colleague, a neighbour or a relative. It had two or more people in it, and they didn't all agree about what happened.
card.goal: Retell the story in two or three minutes. Report fairly what each person said, and what they meant. Then answer your listeners' questions.

phrases: You'll never believe what my colleague told me.
Apparently, they'd been arguing about it for weeks.
It turned out that nobody had checked the booking.
She said that … , but he denied it.
prepare.notes: Write the sequence of events in five short lines. Next to each person's name, write what they said and what you think they meant.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, retell your story to a small group. Each listener asks you one question about the order of events, or about what someone meant. Your teacher listens for fair reporting verbs and for the perfect forms.
doIt.wehel: Let's practise retelling a story. I will tell you a story I heard from someone else. Listen, then ask me questions: what happened first, who said what, and what they meant. If I use a reporting verb that is not fair, like claimed when there is no reason to doubt, point it out. At the end, tell me if my story was clear.

model.title: The missing laptop
lines: You'll never believe what my neighbour told me yesterday.
Samir had been waiting all week for a new laptop. The tracking said it had been delivered, but there was nothing at his door.
Oh no. Had someone stolen it?
That's what he thought. Apparently, he went straight to the woman next door, Ana, and asked if she'd taken it in.
She denied it. She said she'd been at work all day. But Samir said another neighbour had seen her with a big box.
Well, it turned out that the box was hers. She'd ordered a new chair. Samir's laptop had been left at the wrong address, three streets away.
What a mix-up! Did he apologise?
He did. And to be fair to him, he wasn't accusing her. What he meant was, he hoped she had it, so it was safe.
Better than ever. They've been laughing about it all week, and he's offered to help her build the chair.
compare: Did you start in a way that made people want to listen?
Was the sequence clear, with had or had been for the earlier events?
Did you report each person fairly, with a neutral verb unless there was a reason to doubt?
Did you say what someone meant, not only what they said?

canDo: I can tell a story that keeps people listening.
I can use the four perfect forms to make the order of events clear.
I can report what people said with claimed, admitted, urged and denied, and choose the verb fairly.
I can compare two accounts of the same event, and write it from two points of view.
I can retell a story I heard, saying fairly what each person said and meant.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is telling the story? Do you think they will be fair to everyone in it?
reading.talk: Choose one event in the text and tell it from the point of view of a different person in the story. What would they say, and what would they mean? Write four or five sentences, or tell Wehel.

quiz.q: I ___ for an hour when the bus finally came.
quiz.why: An activity up to a moment in the past: had been + -ing.

quiz.q: It turned ___ that he'd been waiting at the wrong station.
quiz.why: It turned out that… gives the surprise: what was really true.

quiz.q: He ___ breaking the window, but the camera showed him doing it.
quiz.why: Deny means to say that something is not true.

quiz.q: The union ___ its members to vote before Friday.
I bumped into my old boss on holiday in Rome. What a ___ !
quiz.why: A coincidence is when two things happen together by chance.

quiz.q: Out of the ___ , an old friend rang me after ten years.
quiz.why: Out of the blue means suddenly and unexpectedly.

quiz.q: A report that only gives one side of the story is ___ .
quiz.why: Biased means unfairly supporting one side.

quiz.q: A: You're from Spain, aren't you? B: I'm from Portugal, ___ .
quiz.why: Actually corrects what someone thought, gently.

quiz.q: I think I ___ the instructions. I pressed the wrong button.
quiz.why: mis- means wrongly: I read them wrongly.

quiz.q: Whether we eat outside depends ___ the weather.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Mei's story in pairs, then each learner tells a short mix-up story that starts with You'll never believe… Listeners react and ask one question each. Then build a timeline on the board to practise the four perfect forms.
Day 2: the task. Each learner retells a story they heard, reporting what each person said and meant. The group asks about the order of events, and you point out any reporting verb that is not fair.
Day 3: talk about the book and answer questions. Then two learners read their two points of view aloud, and the class decides where the versions agree and where they contradict each other.
